transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-02
Time: 10:00 PST
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Avery Chen (Redwood AE), Samir Patel (Redwood SE), Dana Ortiz (Redwood CSM); Lena Rodriguez, Marcus Lee, Priya Singh, Tom Wu (Novapay)

Summary (auto): Weekly sync to review throughput runs and tuning. Focus on continuous batching and concurrency targets. Agreed next steps and owners.

00:00 Avery Chen: ok everyone thanks for joining for the weekly POC sync. Quick roll call — we have Samir on the line for the tuning deep dive, Dana from our side to keep the schedule, and from Novapay Lena, Marcus, Priya and Tom. Can you confirm?
00:12 Lena Rodriguez: yep, yep hello all, here
00:18 Marcus Lee: here, Marcus — thanks
00:20 Priya Singh: present
00:22 Tom Wu: hey all
00:30 Avery Chen: great, quick agenda: 1) review the 48 hour benchmark Samir put up, 2) discuss observed queueing and concurrency spikes, 3) proposed tuning (batch window, prefix cache), 4) next steps. Samir you wanna kick off?
00:45 Samir Patel: sure, thanks. So recap quickly — last week we ran three concurrent target profiles: 500, 800, and 1200 concurrent requests. The baseline was your hosted setup hitting Redwood Dedicated via our routing policy. We saw steady throughput up to ~650 qps in the 500 test, but in the 800 test we observed periodic queueing spikes and p99 tail latency jumped. The collector charts are in the spreadsheet link I shared earlier — I think Tom posted it in the thread?
01:15 Tom Wu: yeah I put the spreadsheet in the slack thread, link is in the invite but also https://redwood.ai/novapay/throughput-spreadsheet (note: internal link)
01:30 Samir Patel: cool. A couple of notes — there are two levers: continuous batching window (we increased from 5 ms to 12 ms for some runs) and per-worker concurrency. Also prefix/KV cache hit rate matters a lot for repeated prompts — your workload is fairly stable so cache helps.
01:55 Marcus Lee: quick q — the KV cache you mean the K V cash — sorry the prefix cache for repeated sessions? How stateful is that for us? We do many short lived chat sessions, not long single convos.
02:10 Samir Patel: good point. For short sessions the benefit is less per-session but across many similar prompts it still helps if you have repeated system messages or templates. We recommend a small prefix cache with aggressive eviction for your pattern. It buys about 8-12% throughput in our runs for Novapay-like traces.
02:35 Priya Singh: were the runs on g4dn or A100? We need to map to our infra notes — we are trying to compare to what we can replicate on prem.
02:45 Samir Patel: these runs were on GCP A2 (A100) instances in Dedicated. The runtime picks kernels differently on A100 vs Ampere, so numbers will shift. For on-prem we can help with a kernel profile. There might be some mis-transcription in the telemetry where "A2" shows up as "A 2", sorry if that threw anyone off in the sheet.
03:10 Lena Rodriguez: ok, the interesting bit was the queueing at ~800 concurrency. Can you walk through what triggers that? Is it batching window size, queue depth, or just worker saturation?
03:25 Samir Patel: it's a mix. At 800 concurrency we saw worker saturation combined with batching inefficiency: the batch packer was creating smaller batches due to skewed inter-arrival times, and once the KV cache miss rate rose the backend compute per request went up, pushing utilization above 90% and the request queue grew. So you get increased latencies and then the packer increases window to accumulate tokens which then hurts tail in other ways.
04:00 Marcus Lee: is there an easy knob we can play to prevent that spike? For example fixed max concurrency at router level or a queue throttle?
04:12 Samir Patel: yes two practical knobs: 1) set per-route concurrency caps in the router to keep worker saturation in check and provide a small queue target; 2) tune the continuous-batching window dynamically — for Novapay we recommended 8-10 ms for steady states, and an adaptive fallback to 5 ms when queue depth increases. That keeps throughput high but avoids runaway queueing.
04:40 Priya Singh: what about deprioritizing long tails like very long contexts? We do have some rare long-document prompts.
04:50 Samir Patel: we can tag long-context requests and route them to a separate pool or throttle them — Redwood's smart routing supports routing by sequence length to a pool with different kernels/instances. That was mentioned in the doc under routing best practices.
05:05 Tom Wu: in the late-night runs we saw memory spikes — maybe due to KV cache growth?
05:12 Samir Patel: likely. Make sure KV cache has eviction based on recency and size; we recommended a 2GB cap for the workload and a 60s TTL for your session prefix use-case. That reduces memory churn.
05:30 Lena Rodriguez: can you show the chart where p99 jumps at 42 minutes into the 800 run?
05:40 Samir Patel: yep pulling up the chart — in the sheet cell G12 we logged p50/p95/p99 by minute. At 00:42 p99 jumps from ~340ms to 1.6s and correlates with an increase in cache misses and a simultaneous spike in batch formation time.
06:05 Marcus Lee: was there cross-traffic from other tenants? We saw some capacity variation in Dedicated at the time window — curious if noisy neighbors might be a factor.
06:18 Samir Patel: Dedicated isolates GPU but network and scheduling can introduce jitter. We flagged the run as "no external noisy neighbors" in the run metadata but there was a background maintenance event in the region reported by the cloud provider — I annotated that in the sheet but it might be partial. We can re-run on a reserved host if you want definitive isolation.
06:40 Priya Singh: re-run would be helpful, but timeline wise we want to get to a pilot threshold in two weeks. Can we prioritize re-run on reserved hosts?
06:50 Avery Chen: yes we can schedule a re-run on reserved capacity; that is one of the benefits of Redwood Dedicated — we can reserve not just pool but host-level isolation for a short window. We'll make that an option and estimate cost impact in the updated spreadsheet.
07:10 Samir Patel: another small tuning: bump worker count a touch and reduce max tokens per request to enforce faster per-token throughput if your use cases tolerate chunking. For example splitting some long completions into two shorter ones reduced p99 in our synthetic tests.
07:35 Tom Wu: hmm that might require app changes. Some of our flows assume an atomic response. Splitting isn't trivial for product.
07:44 Samir Patel: understood — it's an option but not always viable. Second path is queue smoothing: set router to allow short bursts but cap sustained concurrency, plus route long-context calls to a separate pool.
08:05 Lena Rodriguez: are there metrics we should watch live to detect imminent queueing? We want alerts not just postmortem charts.
08:15 Dana Ortiz: on Redwood Console you can set an alert on queue depth and p95 latency, and we can add an anomaly detector for cache miss rate spikes — I'll include a runbook snippet in the notes.
08:30 Samir Patel: yes p95 latency plus worker CPU/GPU util and packer latency are the top 3 signals. If packer latency rises above 10ms consistently it's a sign to reduce window or cap concurrency.
08:50 Marcus Lee: can Redwood share the packer settings you used in the successful 500 test vs the 800 test? We wanna try those as A/B configs.
09:00 Samir Patel: absolutely — I'll export the config diff. In short: 500 test used batch window 6 ms, max batch size 64, adaptive backoff enabled; 800 test had window 12 ms and max batch 128. We'll share the exact JSON in the sheet but note that the runtime may translate names slightly, the packet sometimes shows field names like "batch_ms" vs "batch_window_ms" in older runtime versions.
09:30 Priya Singh: small nit — are there any SLO tradeoffs if we reduce window? i.e. throughput down for tail latency improvement?
09:40 Samir Patel: there is a small throughput hit at the same concurrency if you reduce window, but it tends to lower p99 dramatically. It's a typical latency-throughput tradeoff. With adaptive windowing you get most of the throughput in steady state and avoid the tail spikes.
09:58 Lena Rodriguez: ok good. Wanted to bring up routing policies too — we saw some requests routed to fallback models which have slower kernels and showed up as higher latency. Can we pin model variants for the pilot?
10:12 Samir Patel: yes you can pin model versions per route; pinning prevents automatic fallback to quantized variants unless you enable a model-variant fallback policy. For pilot we recommend pinning to the verified variant to keep numbers consistent. We can enable fallback later for cost experiments.
10:30 Marcus Lee: any delta in throughput when using mixed-precision quantized models vs full fp16?
10:38 Samir Patel: typically quantized models give 1.3-1.8x throughput improvement depending on kernel support; but quality varies and some ops aren't quantization-friendly. Our recommendation: test quantized for cost runs only and keep pilot on fp16.
10:55 Tom Wu: ok, next I think we should talk about telemetry — which traces are most helpful for you to debug these spikes?
11:05 Samir Patel: request tracing with packer timestamps, KV cache hit/miss per request, worker enqueue/dequeue times, and GPU compute durations. Those let us map queueing to compute vs packing inefficiencies. If you can attach a sample of 30-50 trace IDs around the spike window that's ideal.
11:28 Priya Singh: we'll collect that from our env and share; might be noisy but we'll annotate which minutes correspond to the tests.
11:40 Avery Chen: sounds good. Quick recap so we don't lose track: Samir will share tuned config and updated throughput spreadsheet by Thursday 3/4. Marcus will run 24h concurrency tests at 500/800/1200 and upload traces by 3/9. Dana will schedule a latency deep-dive the week of 3/16 with Priya and Samir. Anything else?
12:05 Lena Rodriguez: can Redwood also provide an estimate for reserved-host re-run cost?
12:12 Dana Ortiz: yes I'll include cost estimate as a line item in the spreadsheet and note SLA differences.
12:20 Marcus Lee: one more question — do you have any suggestions around queuing policy at the client side vs letting Redwood's router handle it? We saw client side timeouts that masked the queueing behavior.
12:34 Samir Patel: for diagnosis keep client-side timeouts loose during runs so you capture backend behavior. For production, we often recommend hybrid: short client timeout to surface bad requests and server-side queueing with backpressure signals for graceful requeues. We'll include recommended client SDK configs in the follow-up note.
12:55 Priya Singh: thanks, that's helpful.
13:02 Avery Chen: ok we're at 52 minutes, appreciate the time. We'll send the notes and configs and the spreadsheet update. Meeting adjourned.
